5 Malaise-Era Muscle Cars That Were Quicker Than They Looked
16 photos
Photo: Mecum Auctions
The Malaise Era remains the dark age of American automotive history since it ended unrestricted factory performance and thus the golden age of muscle. But while horsepower dropped significantly during those years, there were still some performance rides that kept American muscle alive.
For American performance enthusiasts, the 1970s started with a bang. That model year, GM lifted its displacement ban on intermediate engines and, along with the rest of the Detroit brands, introduced some of the most powerful factory-built performance models of the era.
However, just three years later, rising insurance rates, new emission regulations, an oil crisis and, last but not least, a switch from gross to net horsepower ratings, had a dramatic impact on the industry and nearly killed off muscle cars .
Until the early 1980s, the American automotive industry went through what automotive journalist Murilee Martin later called (and popularized) the "Malaise Era," a period of emission-driven development that took performance off the list of priorities for most carmakers.
Despite all the drawbacks, several brands continued to deliver some form of performace and, although largely subdued, muscle cars continued to exist. Among those Malaise Era muscle cars were the following five models that didn’t look too muscly but were still decently quick in a straight line.
1974 Chevrolet Chevelle Laguna S-3 454 Photo: Bring a Trailer During the late 1960s and up until 1971, the Chevelle , particularly the performance-oriented SS trim, was one of the most potent and sought-after muscle cars around.
However, for the 1973 model year, the entire model line was redesigned following the new Colonnade styling trend and focusing on emissions and safety.
Because performance was no longer a priority, the SS was now more of an appearance package than a standalone performance model.
Photo: Bring a Trailer Since performance was no longer on the list of priorities, the SS was dropped altogether for the 1974 model year. Nevertheless, the Chevelle lineup did continue to have a strong performer within its ranks.
That strong performer was the Chevelle Laguna S-3, a trim developed for NASCAR homologation, which could be equipped with the optional 454-ci (7.4-liter) Mark IV big-block V8 .
While it didn’t look too sporty despite its NASCAR homologation special status, the Chevelle Laguna S-3 equipped with the 235-hp big block could still run the quarter mile in the low 16s, which, although at least two seconds slower than the golden age Chevelle SS, was pretty quick for a Malaise Era performance ride.
Often forgotten or grossly underrated, the 1974 Chevrolet Chevelle Laguna S-3 454 kept the muscle car torch burning during that dark, emission-friendly-focused era.
1974 Dodge Charger Rallye 440 Photo: Bring a Trailer The Charger debuted in 1966 as a lavish fastback coupe developed specifically to rival AMC’s Marlin in the affordable personal luxury car segment, but in 1968, it was totally redesigned and abandoned personal luxury for a more performance-focused approach.
In 1974, the third-generation Charger, which debuted in 1971 with some serious muscle still on offer, was entering its last year on the market and reached its lowest point in terms of performance.
Nevertheless, there was still a trim that offered more-than-decent performance when equipped with the optional 440 Magnum V8.
Photo: Bring a Trailer That trim was the Rallye, a performance package that debuted in 1972 as a replacement for the iconic R/T.
For the 1974 model year, the Mopar brands were offering the 440-ci (7.2-liter) big-block V8 for the last time and when hiding it under the hood, the Charger Rallye had 275 net hp to play with.
While not as fast as the unchoked 440 Magnum Mopars of 1970 or 1971, the Charger Rallye 440 could run the quarter mile in the high 14-second range, which made it one of the quickest muscle cars of the Malaise Era.
1974 Pontiac GTO Photo: Mecum Auctions Most automotive historians and enthusiasts credit Pontiac with kickstarting the golden age of muscle in 1964 when the carmaker added the GTO performance package to its intermediate Tempest/LeMans range.
Ultra popular from the start, the GTO went on to morph into a standalone model that became one of the most iconic muscle cars of all time.
For 1973, the GM division relegated the GTO to an appearance and handling package for the Colonnade-look LeMans and a year later, it slapped the nameplate on a sportier version of the compact Ventura, the Chevy Nova’s Pontiac-badged twin.
Photo: Mecum Auctions This move drove enthusiasts away from the GTO even further, making the compact model a sales flop and one of the most criticized versions of Pontiac's GOAT.
However, the car wasn’t all that bad. Powered by a 350-ci (5.7-liter) V8 rated at 200 hp, it could still run the quarter mile in the high 15s and low 16s, as shown by multiple independent tests conducted by the era’s most prestigious automotive magazines.
Small and apparently underpowered, this model never looked like it deserved the GTO moniker, but in fact, it one of the most capable muscle cars of the Malaise Era.
1976 Plymouth Volaré Road Runner 360 Photo: Bring a Trailer During the golden age of muscle, Plymouth was one of the brands that produced iconic tire shredders.
The most popular muscle car produced by the Chrysler Corporation division during the late 1960s and early 1970s was, of course, the Road Runner.
Introduced in 1968 as a cheaper, no-frills alternative to the upscale GTX , the Road Runner was a marketing hit that became a muscle car legend.
Photo: Bring a Trailer By the end of the 1975 model year however, Plymouth discontinued the Road Runner as a standalone model and transformed it into an optional package for the compact 1976 Volaré.
While it was not as spectacular as the standalone Road Runners, the Plymouth Volaré Road Runner looked aggressive and performed surprisingly well.
In its most potent guise, it was powered by an optional 360-ci (5.9liter) V8 rated at 170 hp, which allowed it to run the quarter mile in the high 16s. Compared to its predecessors, that was unquestionably slow, but for 1976, it was competitively quick and good enough to the thrill performance enthusiasts who sat behind its steering wheel.
1977 Pontiac Can Am Photo: Mecum Auctions After the disastrous sales flop of the 1974 GTO, Pontiac retired the nameplate and focused on performance in the pony car segment with the Firebird range.
However, for the 1977 model year, the GM division decided to reignite interest in its intermediate lineup with a spiritual successor for the GTO.
Dubbed Can Am, the new model was based on the LeMans Sport Coupe, featured a Grand Prix instrument panel, and was powered by the performance motor found in the Firebird Formula and Trans Am.
Photo: Mecum Auctions That motor was the 400-ci (6.6-liter) Pontiac V8, codenamed W72, which produced 200 hp and gave the Can Am a bespoke shaker hood.
With that engine between its shock towers, the 1977 Pontiac Can Am was tested running the quarter mile in the mid-16-second range, which was more than decent for what was essentially the height of the Malaise Era .
The model actually did very well in terms of sales, with Pontiac receiving over 5,000 orders. However, the division only managed to built a little over 1,370 units due to production issues and discontinued the model.
